children.text: Lubao Church, formally San Agustin Church, was founded in 1572 by Augustinian friars and is one of the oldest churches in Pampanga. It has a stone nave about 82 m long and a five-story bell tower, and the National Museum declared it an Important Cultural Property in 2013.

Lubao is an old town in southwestern Pampanga, about 83 km northwest of Manila. It was a thriving settlement even before the Spaniards arrived, and in 1571 Spanish forces and Augustinian missionaries established themselves here, making it the starting point of missionary work in Pampanga. That is why Lubao is often called the cradle of Kapampangan civilization. At its center stands San Agustin Church, which locals also affectionately call Matuang Pisamban (meaning "old church").

According to the records, the church's founding date is taken to be May 3, 1572, when the Archdiocese of Manila accepted it as a visita (mission chapel) of Tondo. It began as a modest chapel built of light materials such as wood, bamboo and nipa palm, located in the barangay of Santa Catalina. Frequent floods led to its move to the present site in San Nicolas 1st, though sources differ on when, giving either 1597 or 1602. The present brick-and-adobe building was built over the first half of the 1600s and is said to have been finished around 1638. Work continued afterward: the building, damaged in the 1645 earthquake, was enlarged in masonry in 1829, and repairs and interior decoration are recorded in 1877 and 1893.

The church is about 82.45 m long, 21.12 m wide and has walls about 2.46 m thick, making it large even among Pampanga's old churches. The facade is restrained Neoclassical, with a semicircular arched main door flanked by fluted pilasters and a triangular pediment that hides the roof. The bell tower, about 31 m high, has five levels: the lower two are square and the upper three are octagonal. In 2013 the National Museum declared the church an Important Cultural Property.

This church does not rely on showy sights. Its appeal is that it has been rebuilt after wars, earthquakes and typhoons, and worshippers still attend Mass here today. It fits well into a tour of Pampanga's old churches, and since the birthplace house and museum of President Diosdado Macapagal are in the same barangay, it makes a good half-day trip. Kapampangans regard the church as a symbol of local faith and history, and you also get to feel the atmosphere of the plaza and market where residents come and go.
The nave is about
long and about
wide, with walls close to
thick. It is said to have been built with brick, local sand and a binder made with egg whites. Inside, a long nave with a high ceiling opens up before you.

The tidy facade consists of a semicircular arched door, fluted pilasters, a rectangular window above the door, small niches and a triangular pediment. Unlike the ornate decoration of Baroque churches, it is plain and photographs well. Some sources mention a relief of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary on the upper facade, so check it for yourself.
The bell tower, about

high, has an unusual structure: two square levels below and three octagonal levels above. The top of the tower collapsed in the April 2019 earthquake and repair work followed. Check on arrival what the restored tower looks like and whether any section is still under repair.

The National Museum declared this church an Important Cultural Property in August 2013. It was recognized for its significant architectural design and its simple yet solemn retablo behind the altar. Because less than 60% of the original structure remains, it did not receive National Cultural Treasure status.

The nave walls were originally painted by the Italian artists Dibella and Alberoni, and murals showing the life of St. Augustine are thought to date from the 1890s. The central retablo is said to have survived the bombing of World War II intact, while some other decoration was lost in the war.

blocks.title: A history of surviving war and disaster

children.text: The church lived through the 1645 earthquake, occupation by revolutionaries in 1898, use as a hospital for American soldiers in 1899, and the collapse of its dome and roof under Japanese shelling in 1942. Restoration was completed between 1949 and 1954, and it reopened to worshippers. Philippine modern history is layered in a single building. Records also say a strong typhoon damaged it again in 1962, showing how many repairs have shaped its present appearance.

Former president Diosdado Macapagal was born in 1910 in the barangay of San Nicolas in Lubao. His birthplace house still stands, and the President Diosdado Macapagal Museum and Library opened in 2009. It is in the same barangay as the church, so the two are easy to visit together. Check opening hours locally.

Lubao also has the Lubao Bamboo Nature Park in Santa Catalina, the Jose B. Lingad Park and Museum in San Nicolas 1st, and Pradera Verde in Prado Siongco. Events such as the April balloon festival and the Sampaguita Festival have also been held. Dates change every year, so check the municipal announcements.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Church visit and the Macapagal house

children.text: Leave Manila. By public transport, take a northbound highway bus toward Pampanga; by car, use the
SCTEX
expressway.

Arrive in central Lubao and walk around the plaza in front of San Agustin Church to see the facade and bell tower. Look closely at the arched main door and pediment, and at the square and octagonal levels of the tower.
If Mass is not in progress, go inside and take your time with the nave, the central altar and the murals. If worshippers are praying, keep your voice down and do not use a flash.
Have lunch in town. Pampanga is regarded as the culinary heartland of the Philippines, so try at least one Kapampangan dish at a local restaurant.
Visit the Diosdado Macapagal birthplace house and museum in the same barangay. It is safest to check in advance whether it is open and its hours.
On the way back, you can stop at the churches in San Fernando or Bacolor and continue your tour of Pampanga's old churches.

Lubao Church alone takes only 1–2 hours. Adding the Macapagal house and other churches turns it into a half day or a full day. The plaza in front of the church is close to the market and can be crowded at busy hours, so we suggest seeing the church early in the morning first and then walking toward the market.
Lubao is about
83km
from Manila. Buses toward Pampanga and Olongapo, such as Victory Liner services departing from the Caloocan terminal, are known to pass through this area.
Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so allow roughly 2–3 hours to be safe. Routes, fares and schedules change often, so check the operator's announcements.
You can also ride to San Fernando (the provincial capital of Pampanga) and transfer to a jeepney or tricycle.
From Manila, take the expressway north into southern Pampanga and head to central Lubao. Enter the church name (San Agustin Church, Lubao) in Google Maps.
The church is in the town center, so the roads around it are narrow and parking can be hard during Mass. Use nearby open lots or the roadside, and check locally whether parking is available.

You can use Clark International Airport (CRK) or Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL). From Clark you can reach southern Pampanga by taxi or ride-hailing car, but check the exact distance and fare locally.
Tricycles and jeepneys run in central Lubao. The church is in the town center, so you can walk around the plaza area.
The barangay of San Nicolas, home to the Macapagal birthplace house and museum, is close because it is the same barangay, but check the exact walking distance locally.

The visit is mostly indoors, but for walking around the plaza and the exterior the cool, clear dry season is the most comfortable. In March–May, when the midday sun is strong, it is best to visit early in the morning.
In the rainy season sudden showers and floods are frequent. Lubao is a place where the church was moved because of floods long ago, so check road conditions ahead of time in the wet months.

Lubao is a good day-trip destination, so most visitors stay in San Fernando, the provincial capital of Pampanga, or around Angeles and Clark. Hotels and restaurants are far more plentiful there. Angeles and Clark are about
1 hour
away by car, though this varies with traffic.

Pampanga is known as the culinary heartland of the Philippines. In town restaurants and the market, look for local Kapampangan dishes such as sisig and buro. Particular eateries sometimes close or change, so it is best to check locally.
The church is still a place of worship where Mass is held. Avoid Mass times and keep your voice down.
Modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees is best. Wear comfortable sneakers rather than sandals.
Repair work on the bell tower and floor was carried out after the 2019 earthquake. Check before your visit whether the church is open and which sections are under repair.
Take photos inside the church without disturbing worshippers, and turn off the flash.
Check Mass times and opening hours through the archdiocese's announcements or by asking locally.
The Macapagal birthplace house and museum are in the same barangay, so it is efficient to visit them together.
It works well to combine this with Betis Church and Bacolor Church in Pampanga for a one-day route.

If you are curious about the church's architectural history, simply knowing the sequence before you visit enriches the experience: founded in 1572, completed in 1638, bombed in 1942, restored in 1954.
The top of the bell tower collapsed in the April 2019 earthquake and was repaired. Check locally before your visit whether the church is open and which sections are under repair.
Entry and photography by tourists may be restricted during Mass and events.
Check the exact opening hours and any donation requests for entry locally.
In the rainy season, when showers and floods are frequent, leave extra room in your travel plans.
The church is in the town center and traffic is often heavy, so check your return transport times in advance.
Keep your belongings close to your body and avoid displaying valuables.
